entries.expanded_summary: Caramel III (150c) is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates. Unlike kitchen caramelisation alone, this additive is produced as a colour ingredient. Caramel III is the ammonia-caramel type: carbohydrates are heated with ammonium compounds (not sulphites).

entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods and drinks brown to dark-brown colour.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority set a lower daily limit for Caramel III because an ammonia-derived manufacturing by-product caused possible immune-system effects in animals. It found no evidence that the caramel colour itself damages genes or causes cancer. Expected exposure to another manufacturing by-product was not a concern when specification limits were met. The controls therefore focus on the composition of the manufactured colour and its by-products.

entries.expanded_summary: Sodium benzoate (211) helps preserve acidic foods and drinks, including some soft drinks, fruit drinks and sauces. It slows the growth of yeasts, moulds and certain bacteria. It is the sodium salt of benzoic acid, and its effectiveness depends on the product's acidity and formulation.

entries.evidence_copy:
An Australian total-diet study published in 2005 estimated that some high-consuming young children could exceed the acceptable daily intake (ADI) for benzoates, with drinks a major contributor. Average estimated exposures were below half the ADI. The ADI includes a substantial safety margin; exceeding it does not, by itself, demonstrate harm.

In some beverages containing benzoates and vitamin C, small amounts of benzene can form, particularly with heat or light. FDA monitoring found that most tested beverages had no detectable benzene or less than 5 parts per billion. Some higher findings led manufacturers to reformulate. Formation depends on the beverage's formulation and storage conditions, not on E211 alone.

entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority compared two exposure models for 319. A worst-case calculation that assumed foods contained the maximum permitted amount placed some high-consuming toddlers and children above the safety limit. When the authority used reported use levels and analytical results instead, no population group exceeded the limit. The revised estimate shows why maximum legal permission and likely real exposure can lead to different conclusions.

entries.tile_summary: Phosphoric acid is an inorganic acid based on phosphorus.
entries.expanded_summary: Phosphoric acid is an inorganic acid based on phosphorus. Unlike citric or lactic acid, it is not a fruit- or fermentation-derived organic acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade phosphoric acid is manufactured from phosphate mineral starting materials or highly purified phosphorus-derived intermediates.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to acidify foods and drinks and to control pH.
entries.fact_2_copy: It is the parent acid of the phosphate salts used elsewhere in food processing.
entries.evidence_copy: After consumption, the phosphate from 338 joins phosphorus from the rest of the diet. Europe's food-safety authority therefore assessed total exposure rather than treating one drink or additive code in isolation. The group safety value was considered protective for healthy people, but it expressly does not apply to those with moderate or severe loss of kidney function, who may clear phosphorus less effectively. The relevant exposure is total dietary phosphorus, not 338 alone.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.evidence_copy: Public discussion often confuses food-grade carrageenan with poligeenan, but they are different materials. Poligeenan is made using harsh acid and heat treatment, has a much lower molecular weight and is not authorised as a food additive. Estimated intake from 471 contributed only about 0.8–3.5% of recommended daily fat intake at the mean.

entries.expanded_summary: Glycine is the smallest amino acid and is a normal building block of proteins in foods and the human body. As an additive it can contribute mild sweetness, buffering or processing effects.

entries.fact_1_copy: Present in proteins throughout ordinary foods and the body.
entries.fact_2_copy: Glycine has a mildly sweet taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used for flavour, buffering or other technological purposes depending on the product.

entries.expanded_summary: L-Leucine is an essential amino acid found naturally in dietary proteins. As a food additive it can be used for technological functions such as flavour, nutrient formulation or powder handling.

entries.fact_2_copy: Leucine is an essential amino acid, although its role as an additive depends on the product formulation.

entries.expanded_summary: Beeswax is the natural wax secreted by honeybees to build honeycomb. Food-grade white or yellow beeswax is purified and used mainly as a coating or glazing material.

entries.expanded_summary: Carnauba wax is a hard plant wax collected from the leaves of the Brazilian carnauba palm. It is one of the hardest natural waxes used in food.

entries.fact_1_copy: Leaves of Copernicia prunifera, the carnauba palm.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for glossy protective coatings on confectionery, fruit and other foods.

entries.expanded_summary: Shellac is a natural resin secreted by lac insects on host trees. It is refined into a hard, glossy coating used on foods and many non-food products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Resinous lac material produced by insects is collected from branches, cleaned, melted or solvent-refined and formed into food-grade shellac.
entries.fact_1_copy: Insect-derived resin rather than a plant wax.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a glazing and protective coating.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its insect origin can matter for vegan or personal ingredient choices.

entries.expanded_summary: Petrolatum, or petroleum jelly, is a highly refined semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons derived from petroleum. Food-grade material is purified to much tighter specifications than crude petroleum products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by refining and purifying selected petroleum fractions to remove unwanted components and create a stable semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for surface coating, release or glazing functions in specified applications.

entries.fact_2_copy: A synthetic polymer wax rather than a natural wax such as beeswax or carnauba.

entries.expanded_summary: L-cysteine hydrochloride is a salt of L-cysteine, a sulphur-containing amino acid found naturally in proteins. In food processing it is particularly known for changing dough properties.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Modern food-grade L-cysteine can be produced by microbial fermentation or other controlled manufacturing routes, then converted to the hydrochloride salt and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Cysteine is a normal amino-acid component of many proteins.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can act as a flour treatment agent by modifying disulphide bonds in dough proteins.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number does not by itself disclose the manufacturing source, so source-specific dietary concerns require product or supplier information.

entries.expanded_summary: Nitrogen is an inert gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.

entries.expanded_summary: Nitrous oxide is a gas composed of nitrogen and oxygen, best known in food for pressurising and aerating whipped cream.

entries.expanded_summary: Propane is a small hydrocarbon gas widely used as a fuel but also purified for specialised food-propellant use.

entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.tile_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener.
entries.expanded_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener. Its molecule contains a cyclic sulphamate structure and provides sweetness with very little mass compared with sugar.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by multi-step chemical synthesis and converted to the potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Roughly 200 times sweeter than sucrose, depending on the food matrix.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to provide sweetness with little added energy and is often blended with other sweeteners.
entries.fact_3_copy: Blending can reduce aftertaste and produce a sweetness profile closer to sugar.
entries.evidence_copy: A 2025 European review concluded that intake of 950 was unlikely to be associated with cancer, disrupted glucose or insulin control, cardiovascular disease or organ toxicity. It set a daily safety limit of 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight and found that high-exposure estimates were generally below it. The review separately recommended a tighter limit for one manufacturing impurity, distinguishing product-purity control from the safety conclusion on the sweetener itself.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of acesulfame K E950 (2025)

entries.fact_3_copy: The same additive number covers cyclamic acid and more soluble sodium/calcium salt forms.

entries.tile_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose.
entries.expanded_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose. It looks and behaves more like a bulk sugar ingredient than an ultra-intense sweetener.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Sucrose is first rearranged enzymatically and then hydrogenated, producing a mixture of hydrogenated sugar alcohols that is purified and crystallised.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ordinary sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Less sweet than sucrose, so it contributes bulk as well as sweetness.
entries.fact_3_copy: Common in sugar-free confectionery because it can provide structure, glassy texture and lower sweetness.

entries.tile_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners.
entries.expanded_summary: Saccharin is one of the oldest high-intensity synthetic sweeteners. It is much sweeter than sugar and is used in very small amounts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled organic chemical synthesis; food products may use saccharin itself or approved soluble salts depending on the formulation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Several hundred times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to provide intense sweetness with negligible bulk.
entries.fact_3_copy: Saccharin has been used as a sweetener since the late 19th century.

entries.tile_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms.
entries.expanded_summary: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by selectively replacing three hydroxyl groups on a sucrose molecule with chlorine atoms. The result is intensely sweet but metabolised very differently from ordinary sugar.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from sucrose through a controlled multi-step chlorination and purification process.
entries.fact_1_copy: Sucrose — ordinary table sugar — is the structural starting point.
entries.fact_2_copy: About 600 times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used for intense sweetness and is relatively stable during many cooking and processing conditions.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority kept the daily safety limit for sucralose at 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight in 2026 and found estimated exposure from currently authorised uses below it in every population group. The same review could not support a proposed extension to more fine bakery products because the many possible baking times and temperatures left a question about forming chlorinated compounds. The reassuring conclusion covers current authorised uses; the unresolved issue concerns a proposed broader high-temperature use.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of sucralose E955 and proposed bakery extension (2026)

entries.fact_1_copy: Thousands of times sweeter than sucrose, so only very small amounts are needed.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an intense sweetener rather than a bulk sugar replacement.

entries.expanded_summary: Thaumatin is an intensely sweet protein obtained from the West African katemfe fruit. Unlike most high-intensity sweeteners, its sweetness comes from a protein rather than a small molecule.

entries.fact_1_copy: Katemfe fruit from Thaumatococcus daniellii.
entries.fact_2_copy: Extremely sweet by weight and also used to modify or enhance flavour.
entries.fact_3_copy: It is a protein sweetener.

entries.expanded_summary: Steviol glycosides are intensely sweet compounds based on steviol, best known from the leaves of the stevia plant. entries.entry_title: Maltitol and maltitol syrup or hydrogenated glucose syrup (965)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups.
entries.expanded_summary: Maltitol and maltitol syrup are sugar-alcohol sweeteners produced from starch-derived maltose or glucose syrups. They provide bulk and texture as well as sweetness.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starch is broken down to maltose/glucose-rich syrup and then hydrogenated; crystalline maltitol or mixed hydrogenated glucose syrup is purified for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: Usually starch-derived carbohydrate syrup.
entries.fact_2_copy: Maltitol is less sweet than sucrose but much closer to sugar in bulk and texture than intense sweeteners are.
entries.fact_3_copy: Widely used in sugar-reduced confectionery and fillings because it supplies body as well as sweetness.
entries.evidence_copy: Maltitol is not fully absorbed, so larger servings can draw water into the bowel and be fermented, causing bloating or loose stools. A United Nations food-additive expert committee did not consider a numerical toxicological limit necessary for its assessed uses. Australia and New Zealand require relevant foods containing polyols to state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. Portion size and the combined amount of polyols matter more than one occurrence of 965 on a label.

entries.expanded_summary: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables. It has sweetness close to sucrose and produces a noticeable cooling sensation in the mouth.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial xylitol is commonly made by hydrogenating xylose obtained from plant hemicellulose; fermentation routes also exist.
entries.fact_1_copy: Industrial xylose can come from wood, corn cobs and other plant fibre streams.
entries.fact_2_copy: Dissolving xylitol absorbs heat, creating the cooling effect familiar in sugar-free gum.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener, particularly in confectionery and oral-care-style foods.

entries.expanded_summary: Erythritol is a four-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and fermented foods. Commercial erythritol is made mainly by fermentation of sugars.

entries.fact_2_copy: About 60–80% as sweet as sucrose, with a cooling sensation.

entries.expanded_summary: Choline salts are forms of choline, an essential nutrient-like compound used by the body to make cell membranes and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Different salt forms are used to make choline stable and practical in formulations.

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars and dextrins.
entries.expanded_summary: Alpha-amylase is an enzyme that breaks starch into smaller sugars and dextrins. The enzyme family occurs naturally across plants, animals and microorganisms; food-grade preparations are commonly produced with selected microbes.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food enzymes are usually produced by controlled fermentation with bacteria or fungi, followed by filtration and purification of the enzyme preparation.

entries.fact_2_copy: Used in baking, brewing, starch processing and other applications where starch needs to be broken down.
entries.fact_3_copy: An enzyme is a protein catalyst, not a conventional small-molecule additive.

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.

entries.expanded_summary: Proteases such as papain, bromelain and ficin are protein-cutting enzymes. These named examples come from papaya, pineapple and fig-family plants respectively.

entries.fact_1_copy: Papain — papaya; bromelain — pineapple; ficin — fig latex.

PLANT_EXTRACT.glyph_brief: Leaf or seaweed frond with a small extraction droplet; neutral, not a health halo.
PLANT_EXTRACT.consumer_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
PLANT_EXTRACT.consumer_examples: Examples: curcumin (100), chlorophylls (140), alginates (400–405) and agar (406).

ANIMAL_DERIVED.glyph_brief: Simple animal/insect origin mark; factual rather than emotive.
ANIMAL_DERIVED.consumer_definition: Starts with animal or insect material. The target substance is separated from that material and then cleaned, refined or converted into a stable food-grade form.
ANIMAL_DERIVED.consumer_examples: Examples: cochineal/carmine (120), bone phosphate (542), beeswax (901) and shellac (904).

FERMENTATION.glyph_brief: Fermentation vessel with small microbe/bubble cue.
FERMENTATION.consumer_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
FERMENTATION.consumer_examples: Examples: riboflavin (101), natamycin (235), xanthan gum (415) and MSG (621).

MINERAL_INORGANIC.glyph_brief: Crystal or salt-grain cue rather than laboratory-warning imagery.
MINERAL_INORGANIC.consumer_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
MINERAL_INORGANIC.consumer_examples: Examples: calcium carbonate (170), iron oxides (172), sodium bicarbonate (500) and phosphoric acid (338).

MODIFIED_NATURAL.glyph_brief: Natural-material cue with clear transformation arrows.
MODIFIED_NATURAL.consumer_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
MODIFIED_NATURAL.consumer_examples: Examples: modified starches (1400-series), methyl cellulose (461), propylene glycol alginate (405) and glycerol esters of wood rosin (445).

CHEMICAL_SYNTHESIS.glyph_brief: Neutral laboratory reaction flask or reaction vessel; no hazard symbol.
CHEMICAL_SYNTHESIS.consumer_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
CHEMICAL_SYNTHESIS.consumer_examples: Examples: quinoline yellow (104), benzoic acid (210), acesulphame potassium (950) and sucralose (955).

CONTROLLED_PROCESS.glyph_brief: Transformation vessel with heat/reaction arrows, showing deliberate change rather than a generic gear.
CONTROLLED_PROCESS.consumer_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
CONTROLLED_PROCESS.consumer_examples: Examples: caramel colours (150a–150d), vegetable carbon (153) and tartrate salts (335–337).

BIOLOGICAL_ENZYME.glyph_brief: Protein/enzyme cue showing a molecule being cut or transformed.
BIOLOGICAL_ENZYME.consumer_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
BIOLOGICAL_ENZYME.consumer_examples: Examples: alpha-amylase (1100), proteases such as papain and bromelain (1101), lipases (1104) and lysozyme (1105).

FOOD_GAS.glyph_brief: Gas cylinder or clean bubble cue.
FOOD_GAS.consumer_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
FOOD_GAS.consumer_examples: Examples: carbon dioxide (290), nitrogen (941) and nitrous oxide (942).

PETROLEUM_REFINED.glyph_brief: Oil-drop or refinery-source cue; factual, not a pollution or hazard icon.
PETROLEUM_REFINED.consumer_definition: Starts with material from crude-oil refining, then undergoes extensive refining and purification to meet food-grade specifications. The petroleum origin remains factual even though the finished material is highly purified.

VARIABLE.glyph_brief: Two or more branching source-route arrows.
VARIABLE.consumer_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
VARIABLE.consumer_examples: Examples include carotene (160a), lecithin (322), glycerol (422) and fatty-acid salts (470).
